\chapter{Synthesis --- The Gift and the Motive}
\label{ch:synthesis-por-para}
\hlchaptermodality{158}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can change the meaning of a sentence by choosing between por and para.}

Complete ES-C51-sintesis-regalo-motivo: say the dinner sentence both ways and say what a wrong choice actually produces.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — the gift and the motive}

\label{lesson:ES-C51-sintesis-regalo-motivo}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Para ti} or \emph{por ti} — one of them is a present and one of them is a reason. Which is which?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Read this twice, changing only one word.

\begin{quote}
— \emph{Hago la comida \textbf{para} ti.} — \emph{Gracias.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
— \emph{Hago la comida \textbf{por} ti.} — \emph{…gracias.}
\end{quote}

The first is somebody cooking you dinner. The second is somebody telling you they are cooking \textbf{because of} you — which, depending on the day, is an act of love or a small complaint.

Two letters. Nothing else in the sentence moved.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a preposition carrying the feeling}]
This is the first place in the book where \textbf{the smallest word in the sentence carries its emotional content}.

Nouns and verbs have been doing the meaning until now. Here the noun is the same, the verb is the same, the person is the same — and the sentence changes completely on a preposition. That is worth meeting deliberately, because English speakers arrive expecting the little words to be plumbing.

They are not plumbing here. \emph{Por} and \emph{para} are the difference between \emph{I made this for you} and \emph{I made this because of you}, and no amount of context repairs the wrong one: your listener will simply hear the thing you did not mean.

Which is also the reassuring part. If you pick the wrong one, you have not produced nonsense or bad grammar — you have said something true about a different situation. Somebody will look faintly puzzled, and you will notice, and that is how this stops being difficult.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} both versions of the dinner sentence, and hear the second one land differently
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Para ti} — a gift or a reason? (A \textbf{gift}.) \emph{Por ti}? (A \textbf{reason}.) And what happens if you choose wrong? (You say something \textbf{true about a different situation} — and somebody will look puzzled, which is how you learn it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
